correctness.rationale: The penultimate map collapses exactly one vertex. Translate that vertex to (0,0) by flipping coordinates. Collapsing it to its diagonal opposite gives worst ratio b/a (the two incident edges give b/a and a/b); collapsing it across the short edge gives 1+a/b (the incident long edge maps to a diagonal); collapsing across the long edge gives 1+b/a. The other pairs are fixed or give smaller ratios. Thus no ordering can beat min{b/a,1+a/b}. Order O,X,Y,Z as in the record: the second map fixes O and X and sends Y,Z to O. It is nonexpansive on all four cycle edges and hence on their shortest-path metric. The penultimate map can send Z to O or Y at the two desired costs, and both images are in the same second-map fiber as Z, proving commutativity. Constant and identity maps cause no restrictions. The branch switch at b/a=phi and the nonexpansive condition b=a follow exactly. This symbolic argument, not sampled weights, proves the real-parameter result.
residual_risks: Only point maps on the four vertices with opposite edges of equal weight; not continuous rectangles or arbitrary linear coordinate projections. The recorded finite checker is not an independent execution or a formal proof.

value.rationale: This is the basic two-coordinate test for sharp constants of commuting point retractions on weighted products. Unlike the unit-weight binary case, every positive unequal weighting forbids a nonexpansive filtration, even though the optimum tends back to 1 as the anisotropy grows. The exact bottleneck and the change of optimal collapse give a usable sharp obstruction for this class of metrics, not a claim about arbitrary Schauder bases. The golden-ratio value is a consequence of the invariant, not the reason for its value.
residual_risks: No extension to larger weighted products or to arbitrary linear bases is established.
